blocks.title: Interference
blocks.text: The superposition of two waves having the same frequency and travelling in the same direction results in a phenomenon called interference.

An experimental set-up to observe the interference of sound waves is shown in Fig. 7.5(a). Two loudspeakers S1 and S2 act as two sources of harmonic sound waves of a fixed frequency produced by an audio generator (AG). Since the two speakers are driven from the same generator, they vibrate in phase; such sources of waves are called coherent sources. A microphone attached to a sensitive cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO) acts as a detector of sound waves; the CRO is a device that displays the input signal as a waveform on its screen. The microphone is placed at various points, turn by turn, in front of the loudspeakers (Fig. 7.5b).

blocks.alt: An audio-frequency generator drives an amplifier that feeds two loudspeakers S1 and S2 set apart. A microphone is moved along a line in front of them and is connected to a CRO. Lines from S1 and S2 to the microphone show the two paths of the sound.
blocks.caption: Two loudspeakers, a microphone and a CRO to observe interference of sound (original diagram after Figure 7.5a).

blocks.alt: Circular wavefronts spread from two sources S1 (red) and S2 (blue) and overlap below them. Green dots mark loud points where crests meet crests and grey dots mark quiet points where crests meet troughs. A note gives the rule: loud for a path difference of n lambda.
blocks.caption: Overlapping waves from two sources: loud and quiet points (original diagram after Figure 7.5b).

blocks.text: At points P1, P3 and P5 a compression meets a compression and a rarefaction meets a rarefaction, so the displacements of the two waves add up according to the principle of superposition and a large resultant displacement is seen on the CRO screen (Fig. 7.5c). From Fig. 7.5(b) the path difference between the waves at P1 is delta S = S2P1 - S1P1 = 4.5 lambda - 3.5 lambda = lambda; similarly at P3 and P5 the path difference is zero and -lambda, where lambda is the wavelength, the distance between any two successive solid or dashed lines.

blocks.title: Constructive interference
blocks.text: Whenever the path difference is an integral multiple of the wavelength, the two waves are added up; this effect is called constructive interference. The condition is delta S = n lambda, where n = 0, +/-1, +/-2, +/-3, ...

At points P2 and P4 a compression meets a rarefaction, so that they cancel each other's effect according to the principle of superposition and the resultant displacement becomes zero (Fig. 7.5d). The path difference between the waves at P2 is delta S = S2P2 - S1P2 = 4 lambda - 3.5 lambda = lambda/2; similarly at P4 the path difference is lambda/2.

blocks.title: Destructive interference
blocks.text: At points where the displacements of two waves cancel each other's effect, the path difference is an odd integral multiple of half the wavelength; this effect is called destructive interference. The condition is delta S = (2n + 1) lambda/2, where n = 0, +/-1, +/-2, +/-3, ...

blocks.alt: Two CRO screens. (c) At a loud point the trace is a large wave: constructive interference. (d) At a quiet point the trace is almost a flat line: destructive interference.
blocks.caption: CRO traces: large at a loud point (constructive), flat at a quiet point (destructive) (original diagram after Figures 7.5(c) and 7.5(d)).

blocks.title: Example 7.1
blocks.text: Two speakers 3.0 m apart emit a constant tone of 344 Hz. A microphone P is moved along a line parallel to, and 4.0 m from, the line joining the speakers. A tone of maximum loudness is heard and displayed on the CRO when the microphone is at the centre of the line and when it is directly opposite each speaker. Calculate the speed of sound. Solution: S1S2 = 3.0 m, f = 344 Hz, distance to the line of motion of P = 4.0 m, v = ?. For maximum loudness the path difference must be 0, +/-lambda, +/-2 lambda, ...; at the middle point O the path difference is zero (S1O = S2O), so constructive interference occurs there. At the next point P of constructive interference the path difference should be lambda: lambda = S2P - S1P. From the right-angled triangle S1S2P, S2P = sqrt((S1S2)^2 + (S1P)^2) = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 m. Therefore lambda = S2P - S1P = 5 - 4 = 1 m. As v = f lambda, v = 344 x 1 = 344 m s^-1.

blocks.title: Example 7.2
blocks.text: The wavelength of a signal from a radio transmitter is 1500 m and the frequency is 200 kHz. What is the wavelength for a transmitter operating at 1000 kHz, and with what speed do the radio waves travel? Solution: lambda1 = 1500 m = 1.5 x 10^3 m, f1 = 200 kHz = 2.0 x 10^5 Hz, f2 = 1000 kHz = 1 x 10^6 Hz. Since the speed of both signals is the same, v = f1 lambda1 = 2.0 x 10^5 x 1500 = 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1; also v = f2 lambda2, so lambda2 = v/f2 = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1 / 1 x 10^6 Hz = 3 x 10^2 m.

A thin soap film illuminated by white light produces an interference pattern (Interesting Fact). Sodium chloride in a flame gives out pure yellow light; this light is monochromatic, not a mixture of red and green (For Your Information).

blocks.prompt: What are the conditions for interference to occur, and what are coherent waves and coherent sources (short questions 7.1, 7.3)? Differentiate between constructive and destructive interference (short question 7.2).
blocks.explanation: The sources must be coherent, that is, of the same frequency with a constant phase difference (for example two speakers driven by one generator); the waves should be of the same kind, of nearly equal amplitude, and overlap in the same region. Constructive interference occurs where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, so crest meets crest (compression meets compression) and the amplitude grows; destructive interference occurs where it is an odd number of half wavelengths, so crest meets trough and the waves cancel.

items: Interference: superposition of two waves of the same frequency travelling the same way. Coherent sources (one generator, in phase) and a microphone on a CRO: constructive where delta S = n lambda (large trace), destructive where delta S = (2n + 1) lambda/2 (no trace).
Example 7.1: S2P = 5 m, lambda = 1 m, v = 344 m s^-1. Example 7.2: v = 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1, lambda2 = 300 m.
